courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Training: the loss, clone, split, prune and opacity reset
md: Densification is driven by the *positional* gradient, not by the photometric error at a pixel directly. A region can look wrong yet not densify if its Gaussians are not being pushed around, which is one reason poorly observed regions stay blurry.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: One final score hides where the gain came from
md: An ablation turns one end-to-end number into a per-component account: what each stage adds, on the same queries and labels, under the same settings. Without it, you cannot tell which stage earns its latency.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
md: A common misconception: "the user can only reach this page through a link we show them, so it is protected". The server receives raw HTTP requests. Anyone can type any URL, edit any parameter and replay any request with tools like curl. Hiding a link is not access control.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Multi-tenant isolation: tenant ids everywhere, row-level security
md: Two RLS traps. First, if the app connects as the table owner or a superuser, the policies are silently skipped. Second, with a connection pool (open database connections the app reuses across requests), set the tenant with `set_config(..., true)` or `SET LOCAL` inside the request's transaction so it cannot leak into the next request that reuses the connection.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberos from zero: KDC, tickets, krbtgt and the PAC
md: Kerberos runs on keys derived from passwords. The TGT is locked with krbtgt's key; each service ticket is locked with the key of the account owning the SPN; the PAC inside carries groups and two signatures. Nearly every Kerberos attack is 'get one of those keys' or 'abuse who may ask for which ticket'.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: ACL abuse and attack paths: the directory as a graph
md: AD permissions form a graph of who can control what. Attackers chain small rights into paths to Domain Admins; BloodHound shows the same graph to defenders. Remove the edges into Tier 0, then alert on permission, membership and password-reset changes. To respond, revert the change, reset any account whose password, SPN or RBCD attribute was written, and use 5136 history to find what else that subject changed.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Inside an OLE file: the compound file format by hand
md: Extensions lie in both directions. A file named `.doc` can really be RTF, OOXML, XML or MHTML, and olevba checks the type from the content before parsing. A file named `.txt` can be an OLE file. Always sniff the bytes first.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Anti-debugging and anti-VM: recognising checks and getting past them
md: Evasion is evidence. A sample that checks for debuggers and virtual machines is telling you it has something to hide. Record every check you find as a behaviour (T1622, T1497) in the report, with the branch it controls.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: When control flow stays legal: data-only attacks
md: CFI answers "is this jump allowed?" Data-only attacks never make a disallowed jump. Defences must also protect the data that decisions depend on, and the most complete answer is still not having the memory bug.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Detecting C2: beacons, egress and fingerprints
md: Regular is not the same as malicious. Software updaters, monitoring agents and chat clients poll on timers too. A beacon score is a hunting lead, ranked with rarity of the destination and the type of host, not an alert on its own. Allowlist known pollers by destination and process, and review the list, because an intruder can hide behind an allowlisted name.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: An agent benchmark score is a property of **model + harness + environment + grader + metric**. Change any one and the number moves. Most of this course is about how each part shapes the score.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: A minimal harness: stop conditions, errors and budgets
md: Do not retry a tool blindly. Re-running a failed `git push` or a payment call can duplicate a side effect. Retry the model API transport freely, but report tool failures back to the model and let it decide, or make the tool itself idempotent, meaning running it twice has the same effect as running it once (for example, a payment call that carries a unique request key the server uses to ignore duplicates).

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion
md: Deletion must follow lineage. Keep source pointers on every derived memory (Generative Agents already stores the cited records for each reflection) so that deleting a source can find and rewrite or delete every reflection, summary and merged fact that contains it. Also delete the embeddings and any copies in logs.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
md: A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Getting data out: images, links, tool calls
md: For every LLM feature, list the ways out: rendered images, links, tools that make network requests, and the user. Close the ones you do not need and allowlist the rest. Without a way out, stolen context stays put.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
md: Poisoning is a supply chain attack on data. Verify integrity with hashes, record provenance, and treat a model from an unknown trainer like a binary from an unknown publisher.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: GNoME: active learning with DFT, and what counts as new
md: Active learning turns DFT from a verifier into a teacher: each round's results, including failures, retrain the filter, so the hit rate per DFT call keeps rising.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
md: Distortion-free per token is not the same as diverse. Because r is a deterministic function of the key and the last few tokens, the same prompt and context always produce the same output, which a user who asks twice can notice. The next block shows Kuditipudi et al.'s fix.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Replay is open-loop: the program's computation between calls is gone, so cache contents and timing differ, and cycles per call in replay are not the application's allocator time. Use replay for memory comparisons and relative call costs, and confirm with a real run.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: Anomalies in the history contaminate the baseline. If last Tuesday's outage is in the training window, a mean-based baseline and standard deviation absorb it and become blind to the next one. That is why both the toy baseline here and S-H-ESD use medians and MAD: one bad day out of 27 does not move a same-hour median.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Rate limits, quotas and resource exhaustion
md: Limits enforced only at one gateway disappear on any path that skips the gateway: a beta host, an internal route, an old API version. Apply the limit in the service, or make sure every route goes through the gateway.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: JWT anatomy: header, payload, signature and base64url
md: A JWT is readable by anyone and trustworthy only after the signature and claims are checked by the receiver, using keys and rules the receiver chose. Everything in it, including the header, is attacker-controlled until then.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: What an application security programme is, and who owns what
md: A programme is owners plus deadlines plus measurement. For every activity in this course, ask three questions: which named person or team does it, by when, and which number shows that it actually happens?

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SAST in CI: false positives, triage and developer trust
md: A suppression is a risk acceptance. If anyone can add `nosemgrep` without review, the cheapest way to pass CI is to silence the tool. Route suppressions in sensitive paths through CODEOWNERS (lesson 1) so AppSec sees them.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Patch SLAs, exceptions and the race after disclosure
md: An exception without an expiry date is a permanent vulnerability with paperwork. Track exceptions as their own metric: how many, how old, and how many were renewed more than once.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: Tuning tradeoffs follow directly from the passes. Rare checkpoints and slow background page writes make the smallest recLSN old, so redo scans more log. Long-running transactions make undo long and keep old log needed. Frequent checkpoints shorten redo but cost extra log and page writes at runtime.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: A semaphore limits **how many** requests are in flight, not **how fast** they start. Concurrency times the inverse of latency gives your request rate, so when latency drops (short prompts, cache hits) the same semaphore sends requests faster. Pair it with a rate limiter, covered next.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: Async Rust in one breath: `async fn` compiles to a lazy state machine; `poll` advances it until an await is Pending; the waker plus the epoll-based driver decide when to poll again; Tokio's workers spread tasks with local queues and stealing; and because nothing preempts a task, every task must reach a Pending await often, or move blocking work to `spawn_blocking`.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Embeddings as features: VGGish, YAMNet and PANNs
md: Split by clip (or by source recording), never by patch. Patches of one clip overlap by 50% and share the same label, so a random patch-level split puts near-copies in train and test and inflates accuracy. ESC-50 ships 5 folds for this reason, and the TensorFlow tutorial carries each clip's fold number along with every patch embedding and splits by fold.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Precomputed tables, rainbow tables, and why salts defeat them
md: A salt does nothing against an attacker focused on *one* account. With a single salted SHA-256 hash, the attacker simply runs their guess list with that salt at full GPU speed. Salting is necessary but not sufficient: the hash must also be slow, which is lesson 5.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Real-time phishing proxies and help-desk social engineering
md: Training people to spot fake pages helps, but NIST defines phishing resistance as working *without relying on the user's vigilance*. The Twitter employees were busy, remote, and called by someone who knew personal details about them.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Evaluating research agents without fooling yourself
md: An LLM judge grading an LLM agent can share its blind spots. Validate the judge against human labels (as JudgeEval does), keep humans testing edge cases, and read transcripts: a high score with a shortcut in the logs is a failed run.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: C++ binaries: name mangling, vtables and RTTI
md: RTTI is useful evidence, not proof. Typeinfo name strings like `N3geo4RectE` survive stripping, and the vtables they point to let you list every polymorphic class and its virtual methods. But builds can disable RTTI (`-fno-rtti`), and malware authors can pick misleading class names. Confirm with constructors (which store the vptr) and with the code itself.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
md: "Matmul becomes additions" applies to the weight matrices. Attention scores (queries Q times keys K, then the attention weights times values V) multiply activations by activations, so they are not ternary. And the speedup only appears with a kernel that actually exploits ternary weights, which lesson 5 covers.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: `cmov` with a memory operand always reads memory, even when the condition is false (the Intel pseudocode does `temp := SRC` first and lists page faults as possible). So a compiler cannot turn `p ? *p : 0` into a cmov from `*p`: it would fault on a null pointer. C's `?:` only evaluates the chosen side; branchless code evaluates both.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Leveled: low space and read amplification, high write amplification. Tiered: low write amplification, more runs to read and up to about 2x temporary space during a full merge. The size ratio T slides each policy along its curve.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Resilience, continuity and recovery: the words and the plans
md: A disaster recovery plan is not a business continuity plan. The DRP brings systems back at another site; the BCP keeps the business working while they are gone, often by hand. Maersk staff booked containers through WhatsApp and personal Gmail during NotPetya: that was continuity without systems, improvised because it was not planned.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups nobody restored: monitoring and testing that prove recovery
md: A green backup dashboard measures jobs, not recovery. Measure what a restore needs: the latest *verified restorable* point (your real RPO) and the last measured restore time at full size (your real RTO). Restore time grows with data size, so a test on last year's volume says little about today's.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When recovery tools fail too: CrowdStrike 2024, keys and break-glass
md: A recovery key stored only inside the thing it recovers is not a recovery key. The same goes for admin passwords in a vault that runs on the failed platform, runbooks on the wiki that is down, and an on-call rota in the chat tool that is offline.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Bytes remove the vocabulary and its blind spots, but multiply the number of positions by roughly 4. Since compute is about $2mT$, a byte model is only practical if the big network runs on far fewer positions than there are bytes.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Byte models trade a tokenizer for an extra design choice: how to group bytes. With learned, entropy-based patches, BLT matched BPE models at 8B for equal training FLOPs, improved robustness and spelling, and turned patch size into a knob that trades steps for model size.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: Audit unsafe code at the module boundary. Keep fields that unsafe code trusts private, check every invariant before the unsafe block (as `assert!(mid <= len)` does), and write a SAFETY comment that names the invariant.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: Arrange data so that what you use together sits together, and walk it in address order. Stride 1 is the cheapest pattern there is.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a transformer as circuits: residual paths, QK and OV
md: A head is two circuits. QK, built from $W_Q^\top W_K$, picks where to look; OV, built from $W_O W_V$, picks what to copy. With patterns frozen, the whole model is a sum of linear paths through OV and residual connections.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: A low CTR at rank 4 does not mean a document is less relevant than one at rank 1. CTR mixes two things: how often the slot is seen and how good the document is. You must separate them before clicks can serve as relevance labels.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stored XSS and the worms it made: Samy and TweetDeck
md: Both worms are stored XSS that spread because the payload could use the victim's session to store itself again. Both trace back to a gap in **output encoding**: a filter that guessed at browser parsing (MySpace) and one rendering path that skipped escaping (TweetDeck). Encoding has to happen on every path, as the very last step before data enters HTML.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Why CLIP learns from captions instead of fixed labels
md: CLIP does not learn to describe images. It learns two encoders whose outputs agree: a matching image and caption land close together in one shared vector space, and non-matching ones land apart. Everything else in this course (zero-shot classification, retrieval, the failure modes) follows from that geometry.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Blind spots: data events, flow logs and traffic you never see
md: Misconception: "VPC Flow Logs record every packet on the network". They record summaries per flow, aggregated over up to 10 minutes by default (1 minute on Nitro instances), and they skip whole categories of traffic, including the instance metadata service and Amazon DNS.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Snowflake 2024 and SaaS platforms: hunting from the customer's side
md: Misconception: "the vendor was not breached, so this is the vendor's problem". In both Snowflake 2024 and Salesloft Drift 2025, the evidence, the containment levers (users, network policies, tokens, secrets) and the exposure decision sat with each customer.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Serverless: execution roles, event injection and function secrets
md: Serverless removes servers, not responsibility. A function is code plus a role plus its triggers: validate every event as untrusted input, give each function only the role it needs, and keep secrets in a secret store rather than in configuration.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: How AWS decides: explicit deny, SCPs, boundaries and resource policies
md: "We added an Allow, so it should work" is the classic debugging trap. If anything anywhere has a matching `Deny`, including an SCP you cannot see from inside the account, no Allow will help. AWS's documentation advises asking your organization's administrators when an SCP might be the cause.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Incident response for a leaked cloud key
md: For a leaked key: deactivate first, then investigate with CloudTrail across all Regions, then hunt for persistence (new users, keys, roles and policies) before declaring it closed. Then remove the reason a long-lived key existed at all.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Agglomerative clustering: linkages and the dendrogram
md: The scikit-learn guide warns that agglomerative clustering has a "rich get richer" behaviour that leads to uneven cluster sizes, with single linkage the worst and Ward the most regular. Its linkage comparison example adds that single linkage "performs poorly in the presence of noise" while Ward is "the most effective method for noisy data".

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: A selection vector is not a filtered copy. Downstream primitives read the original vectors at the listed positions. That avoids copying, but the reads are now indirect and sparse, which matters for SIMD (next lesson).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
md: Vectorization processes several elements per instruction, but only when the compiler can prove it is safe: known trip counts and non-overlapping pointers help. -O2 in GCC vectorizes only the easy cases (no runtime checks, and before GCC 15 no epilogue); -O3 also takes loops that need runtime alias checks.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Measure it: benchmarking builds and an end-to-end tuning run
md: Misconception: "fewer instructions or higher IPC means faster." Here -O0 had the best IPC and the worst time, and -O2 versus -O3 showed a 60 ms median gap with identical instructions. Time is the result; instructions, IPC and cache misses are clues that explain it.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: An atomic load followed by an atomic store is **not** an atomic read-modify-write. The fix here is `num.fetch_add(1, AcqRel)`, which makes L and S one indivisible step. Atomics remove data races; they do not remove race conditions in your logic.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Why one big ODE step from noise collapses to the mean
md: A diffusion model knows the *local* direction at each point. One-step generation needs the *global* answer: where does the whole trajectory end? A consistency model learns that endpoint directly.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: The goal of consistent hashing: when the set of servers changes, move only the keys that must move, which is about $K/N$ keys for $K$ keys and $N$ servers, and never shuffle keys between servers that did not change.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
md: A missing field scores **1**, the best possible decay value, in both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Profiles with no location beat everyone who lives a few kilometers away. Decide explicitly: require the field with an `exists` filter (it keeps only documents that have a value in that field), index a default value, or accept the behavior on purpose.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: A solver turns a declarative model into search plus propagation plus learning. Your job is the model: tight domains, global constraints instead of many small ones, integer scaling, and a time limit with a status check.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
md: Misconception: "runAsNonRoot is enough". It stops UID 0, but a non-root process with `allowPrivilegeEscalation` left at its default of true can still become root through a setuid binary in the image. Set both, and drop capabilities.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
md: Label every namespace with a Pod Security level: Restricted for applications, Baseline at minimum, Privileged only for reviewed system namespaces. Add a policy engine for rules PSA cannot express, and treat its webhook as critical infrastructure.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
md: Use both views: the audit log for who changed what through the API, and a syscall-level sensor such as Falco for what processes actually do. Each covers the other's blind spot.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Strict mode guarantees the diff is **schema-valid**, not that it is **right**. A perfectly typed `{"remove": []}` for *drop the salary limit* is still a wrong state. Schema enforcement removes parsing failures; only evaluation (lesson 6) catches meaning failures.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Faithfulness is a causal claim about what drove the answer. You test it by intervening, not by reading. A biasing feature that flips answers without ever being mentioned proves the CoT omitted a real cause.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Building and scoring a CoT monitor
md: Misconception: "our monitor has an AUROC of 0.95, so it is good enough." AUROC averages recall over all false-positive rates, including ones no review team could handle. Report recall at the FPR you will actually run, and precision at a realistic base rate.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A bi-encoder pays the document cost once, offline. A cross-encoder pays the full transformer cost for every (query, document) pair at query time. That single fact explains both why it is more accurate and why it can only rerank a shortlist.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Misconception: "nobody knows our format, so it is safe". That is security through obscurity. Formats leak, binaries get reverse-engineered, employees leave. If learning the algorithm breaks your system, it was never secure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
md: Do not use one key for two jobs (say, encryption and MAC, or client-to-server and server-to-client). Derive separate keys with HKDF and distinct labels.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Nonce budgets for AEAD: counters, random nonces, XChaCha, GCM-SIV
md: "Each server picks random nonces, so we are fine" is only true while the total across all servers stays under the cap. Ten servers each sending a billion messages a year under one key pass 2^32 in under six months. Count per key, not per server.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Reviewing crypto code: safe APIs, tests and migration
md: Prefer APIs that remove choices, pin every parameter to the key, test that misuse is rejected, and keep an inventory so that when an algorithm, library or key fails, you know exactly what to rotate.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: More stages are not automatically faster. Each stage costs shared memory that a bigger tile or an epilogue staged through shared memory could use, and once loads are hidden, extra stages add nothing. StageCountAuto simply fills what is left.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: From device to NUMA node: decoders, interleaving and regions
md: Pick the memory zone deliberately. Hot-plugged CXL memory can be onlined as `ZONE_MOVABLE` or `ZONE_NORMAL`. Kernel allocations are generally not migratable and can only use `ZONE_NORMAL` or lower, so CXL memory in `ZONE_MOVABLE` serves only user pages and other movable data. `daxctl` onlines as movable by default; that keeps kernel data off the device but means CXL capacity cannot absorb kernel memory pressure.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: View source is not hacking: the Missouri teachers' SSNs (2021)
md: Reading what a server sends you is not breaking in, but laws differ by state and country, and accusations can come anyway. Collect the minimum to prove a flaw, report it privately, keep records, and wait for the fix.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
md: DMCA 1201 bans circumventing access controls on copyrighted works even without copying; the security research exemption (renewed every three years) covers good-faith research on devices you lawfully own, but not other laws or tool trafficking. Trade secret law cares about where your copy of a secret came from.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
md: ISC2: four canons, enforced through certification. ACM: avoid harm, respect privacy, report risks, access only when authorised. Menlo: respect for persons, beneficence, justice, respect for law and public interest. Ask before you experiment on people, including code reviewers.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
md: A learned weight is a share of a budget, not a property of the domain. Copying published weights to a run 10 times longer silently multiplies every domain's epochs by 10. Always convert weights to epochs for your own budget and data sizes before training.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: SoA is not automatically faster. Its advantage is exactly the fraction of each record that a loop does *not* touch. A loop that uses every field gains nothing from the layout change, and some access patterns get worse (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Finding sensitive data: inventories, patterns, checksums and context
md: A match is evidence, not proof. Pattern plus checksum gives low confidence; only context (keywords, expiry dates, nearby names) raises it. Tune discovery and DLP rules to act on high confidence and review the low-confidence bucket, rather than blocking on every 16-digit number.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security II: auditing reads and the Snowflake thefts
md: Log reads of restricted data, not just changes: pgAudit object logging on sensitive columns, warehouse query history, cloud data events. Alert on sequences (list everything, stage, export, download) and on volume compared with the same account's normal.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
md: A fixed seed proves nothing about kernel determinism, and batch-invariant kernels prove nothing about the sampler. Run two separate experiments: hold the batch fixed and vary the seed to test sampling, and hold the seed fixed while varying batch size and position to test the kernels. A test that varies both at once cannot attribute a failure.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
md: Protecting the workflow file is not enough. With I-PPE the attacker never touches it: they edit what it calls. Treat everything the privileged job executes (Makefiles, scripts, test files, tool configs, lockfiles) as part of the pipeline.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
md: The forward process is fixed and trivial. The only thing to learn is a **mask predictor**: given a partly masked sequence, output a distribution over the vocabulary at every masked position. It needs no timestep input.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
md: An estimate of the bound is not the log-probability. d1's one-pass mean-field estimate is biased by construction, and an ELBO estimate is both a bound and noisy. Methods that work here control that error (shared masks, many timesteps, random prompt masks as regularization); plugging a single random ELBO sample into an AR recipe is what LLaDA 1.5 calls naive DPO.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Chunked prefill bounds interference inside one GPU; disaggregation removes it and lets each phase get its own hardware, parallelism and scale. Pick by measuring per-GPU goodput under your SLOs, prompt lengths and interconnect, not by architecture preference.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Mobile forensics: extraction levels, encryption and isolation
md: Turning a seized phone off "to preserve it" can move it from AFU to BFU and lock most of its data away for good. Decide on power, isolation and extraction before you touch it, and document every interaction.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
md: Choosing: **DiskANN** when the data is far larger than RAM and an SSD is acceptable (a few ms per query at high recall on one machine). **CAGRA** when vectors fit in GPU memory and you need high throughput or fast builds; IVF-PQ initial graph builds can run in batches on datasets larger than GPU memory. **CAGRA then HNSW** when you build on GPUs but serve on CPUs.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: ORPO and SimPO: dropping the reference model
md: "Reference-free" also means there is no explicit KL anchor to the starting model. ORPO's SFT term and SimPO's length normalization and margin are what keep these losses from degenerating, and the SimPO authors stress that hyperparameter tuning matters for every **offline** method (one that trains on a fixed dataset instead of sampling new answers from the policy), DPO included.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Switch reads only when sustained, high-volume comparison shows zero unexplained mismatches, and keep dual writes running so the switch can be undone by a flag.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Estimate cost as event rate x cost per event. Keep the rate low (stable, specific probes; filters; sampling) and keep the work in the kernel (maps, not printf). That is what makes bpftrace usable on a live production system.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords
md: Patching closes the hole. It does not un-leak what already leaked. After any file-read bug on an edge device, rotate every secret the device held and every password typed through it.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate
md: Evidence first, then the fix. Collect what the vendor's procedure allows before patching or rebooting, isolate without powering off once compromise is found, patch, and if compromise is possible rebuild and rotate every secret the device held or saw.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: L1-Exact spends the requested budget even when the problem is easy, because its reward penalizes being too short. When the goal is a worst-case cost cap rather than an exact length, use the Max formulation, which matched or beat L1-Exact while often using up to 2x fewer tokens.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: From antivirus to EDR: sensor, cloud, console and response
md: EDR does not replace logs or antivirus. It adds a recorder on every endpoint, a fleet-wide brain, and a remote hand. Each of the three can fail separately: no sensor, no data; no analytics, no alert; no one watching, no response.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Attack surface reduction rules: blocking risky behaviours
md: Exclusions are the quiet failure. Microsoft warns that excluding files or folders "can severely reduce ASR rule protection" and that excluded files run with **no reports or events recorded**. An exclusion for a whole folder such as a user-writable tools directory turns a rule off for anything an attacker can drop there.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs
md: Do not read CO's perfect toy score as "CO beats event detection". CO was given the exact appliance powers and only three appliances with no sum collisions. Add one appliance whose power equals a sum of others, or real-world power that drifts, and per-sample matching breaks while temporal models degrade more gracefully.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Watch cluster sizes. One low-threshold edge between two big clusters creates a giant cluster that silently merges thousands of records. Alert on clusters that grow suddenly, and require stronger evidence for edges that would join two large clusters.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
md: An app is defined once (application object, home tenant) and instantiated per tenant (service principal). Credentials live with the definition, permissions with the instance. Anyone who can add a credential to a powerful app becomes that app.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
md: In device code flow, the tokens go to whoever started the flow, not to whoever signed in. Block it with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy except where a known device needs it, and hunt for deviceCode in sign-in logs followed by device registrations.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
md: Every component that bridges AD to Entra ID (the sync server and its accounts, PTA agents, the AZUREADSSOACC key, AD FS) can create or impersonate cloud identities. Treat each as Tier 0, roll the Seamless SSO key at least every 30 days, and keep cloud admins cloud-only.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Draining one busy descriptor to `EAGAIN` can starve the others, since a fast sender may never let the buffer empty. epoll(7) suggests keeping your own ready list: mark the connection ready, process a bounded chunk, and round-robin across all ready connections before waiting again.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: A confidence interval or significance test computed on the same queries you used to pick the winner is not valid. Report CIs from a set that played no part in the choice.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: ASLR and PIE: moving the targets on every run
md: Common misconception: "ASLR makes the overflow fail." It does not stop the corruption at all; the attacker still overwrites the pointer. ASLR only makes the *value* they write likely to be wrong. Anything that tells them the right value (next lesson) cancels it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
md: Simplified model: real chips overlap work with store buffers (queues that hold a core's writes while it keeps running) and out-of-order execution (running later independent instructions while an earlier one waits), prefetch lines before they are asked for, and have varying transfer latency by core distance. Use the model for direction and scaling, and measure the actual number on your hardware.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: Secure aggregation hides *who contributed what*. It does not make the result safe to publish: the sum of 100 updates can still reveal a rare phrase typed by one user. For that you need noise, and a budget that accounts for every round you release.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
md: The bias changes **which** experts a token uses, never **how much** a chosen expert contributes, and it receives no gradient. That is how Loss-Free Balancing controls load without fighting the language-modeling objective.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
md: Two classic bugs. First, `kv_last_page_len` is never 0: a request with exactly 8 tokens and page size 4 has 2 pages and last length 4. Second, FlashInfer does not allocate or free pages. Its FAQ says page-table management is the serving engine's job; FlashInfer only computes attention over whatever arrays you pass (int32, per the docs).

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
md: A primed equation is not an assignment; an action is a true-or-false formula about a pair of states. If an action says nothing about a variable, the next value is unconstrained. TLC refuses such a spec: dropping `UNCHANGED tmp` from Write makes it stop with "Successor state is not completely specified by action Write".

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus on real data: views, quantifiers, triggers and failed proofs
md: Write quantified specs so that the terms your proof naturally mentions match the triggers. Relate arbitrary pairs (v[i] <= v[j]) rather than neighbors when the code jumps around, and keep nonlinear or bitwise facts in small by(...) queries.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
md: Not every tensor tolerates coarse grouping. DeepSeek tried quantizing activation gradients in 128x128 blocks (so only a transpose would be needed in the backward pass). A 16B MoE model trained for about 300B tokens diverged: Dgrad feeds every earlier layer in a chain and is very precision-sensitive. Activation gradients keep fine 1x128 tiles.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Abuse economics: make every attempt cost more than it earns
md: Profit per attempt is $s\,v - c$. Every control you add should be able to say which of the three it moves, and by how much, and what it costs honest users.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: CAPTCHAs, their limits and privacy-preserving tokens
md: A CAPTCHA is a price, not a wall. Verify it on the server, bind it to the action, make it single use, show it only when risk is high, and watch its solve rate for signs it has been broken.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card testing, 3-D Secure and strong customer authentication
md: Card testing costs you even when every attempt is declined. Protect every endpoint that can touch a card with server-verified challenges and shaped rate limits, and use 3-D Secure to move risky card-not-present payments onto the issuer's authentication.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake reviews and content abuse
md: Inauthentic content shows as copies and groups: near-duplicate text, bursts, and lockstep reviewer sets. Known harmful media is matched with perceptual hashes against shared lists, never by collecting it yourself.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
md: `synchronous_commit = off` and `fsync = off` sound similar but are not. The first may lose the last ~600 ms (by default) of acknowledged commits and stays consistent. The second can corrupt the whole cluster (PostgreSQL's word for all the databases one server manages) and is only for data you can recreate, such as an initial bulk load.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
md: "Unique crashes" is not a bug count. When a tool, a vendor pitch or your own dashboard reports it, ask how deduplication was done and how many distinct fixes the crashes needed.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far
md: Verified so far: AI agents can find real bugs by variant analysis (Big Sleep, SQLite), AI-written harnesses extend fuzzing coverage and find real CVEs (OSS-Fuzz, OpenSSL), and attackers use AI to find logic flaws (GTIG 2026). In every defensive case, a concrete reproducer and a sanitizer or test confirmed the bug.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
md: Lucene's javadoc documents a surprise: `FuzzyQuery` on `abcd` with `maxEdits=2` does not match the indexed term `ab`, even though the Levenshtein distance is 2. Engines add rules of their own on top of the textbook distance, so test short terms and other edge cases directly.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
md: A match is not the end product. The solver turns matched star pairs into CRPIX, CRVAL and a CD matrix under a TAN projection, which any FITS tool can then use to label every pixel with RA and Dec.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
md: A common misconception is that interpolation conventions only matter for image quality. They also move geometry. If training resized with half-pixel centers and inference resizes without them, every pixel coordinate the model predicts is offset by $(s-1)/2$ source pixels, and no amount of retraining the head (the final prediction layers) fixes a preprocessing mismatch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Forgetting record_stream (or calling s0.wait_stream(s1) before the free, which makes all later work on s0 wait for the work already queued on s1) is a silent data race, not a crash: the new tensor's kernel on s0 may overwrite memory that s1 is still reading. The PyTorch docs note the synchronization is needed even when the side stream only writes.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
md: **Misconception:** the L1 cache makes access patterns irrelevant. Caches help when nearby warps reuse what was over-fetched, as with small misalignments. A large stride over data read once gets no reuse, and every unused byte still crosses the DRAM interface.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Occupancy is a capability, not an achievement. 100 percent occupancy with 5 percent of peak throughput is a latency-bound kernel with plenty of warps and nothing for them to do, and the fix has nothing to do with occupancy.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Occupancy: how many warps fit on an SM at once
md: Higher occupancy is not automatically faster. Low occupancy hurts latency hiding, but past some point extra warps add nothing, and a lower-occupancy kernel can keep more data in registers and avoid spilling (storing values that do not fit in registers out in slower memory). Measure.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: Do not estimate GraphRAG cost from the number of documents alone. Cost scales with total tokens, chunk size, gleaning rounds, the number of entities and relationships that need summaries, and the number of communities. The official docs open with a warning that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources and suggest starting small.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Build it: GRPO on GSM8K with a small model
md: A reward curve can rise while accuracy does not. If the format reward is easier to earn than the accuracy reward, the summed reward climbs as the model learns the tags, and the accuracy part stays flat. Always log each reward function separately, and evaluate on held-out questions with sampling settings you also use at test time.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Polling, caching and data quality in production
md: A common bug is merging realtime messages instead of replacing state. With FULL_DATASET, a trip missing from the newest message must lose its prediction. Merging keeps stale predictions alive for trips that already finished or were dropped by the producer.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Out-of-order and speculative execution, from zero
md: Speculation is safe for *results* and unsafe for *secrets*. The CPU guarantees that mispredicted work never changes what a program computes, but it was never designed to hide that the work happened. Every attack in lessons 7 to 11 is a way to steer transient instructions and then read their footprint.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: CL.TE and TE.CL: two parsers, one stream
md: A desync needs only this: one hop reads **fewer** body bytes than the hop in front of it. The bytes it did not read become the start of the next request on that connection. Reject ambiguous framing at every hop and close the connection whenever framing is in doubt.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Web cache deception: making the cache keep a private page
md: Defence in depth matters here because the origin and the cache are often owned by different teams. The origin team should mark every personalised response `Cache-Control: no-store, private`; the CDN team should make sure no rule overrides that. Either alone has been bypassed in practice.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: `enabled=madvise` turns THP into an opt-in: only regions the application marks with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` get huge pages at fault time. The THP doc recommends it where wasted memory matters, and `madvise(MADV_COLLAPSE)` (Linux 6.1+) lets a program request a synchronous collapse of a range.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Known weak spots from the NVIDIA study: the 16K and 32K hybrids trailed the Transformer by about 1 point on long-context tasks, mostly multi-document QA where distractor passages may confuse the SSM state. Hybrids were also more prompt-sensitive: on MuSiQue the hybrid ranged 10.63 to 16.16 across prompt tweaks vs 15.25 to 17.68 for the Transformer.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
md: Averaging fixes errors that differ from sample to sample. It cannot fix an error every sample shares, such as the LLM misunderstanding an ambiguous or unfamiliar query. That is the root of HyDE's main failure mode in lesson 5.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
md: Secure protocols only help when they are on. An OPC UA server left in mode None, a DNP3 outstation without SAv5 keys, or a Modbus/TCP Security device that also listens on plain port 502 gives the attacker the old, unauthenticated path.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
md: Two IT reflexes can hurt in OT: rebooting or reimaging a running HMI or server (NIST: rebooting 'may not be acceptable'), and running active scans across the control network during an incident. Both can stop the process or the operators' only view of it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: XML signature wrapping: the verifier and the app read different parts
md: One parse, one element. The code that verifies the signature must hand the verified element to the code that makes decisions, and nothing else in the document may be consulted. Any second search of the document, by name, by position or by a second parser, reopens the gap.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Detecting forged federation tokens and recovering trust
md: Resetting passwords, re-enrolling MFA or rebuilding one server does not remove a forged-token capability. Until the signing key is replaced everywhere it is trusted and the attacker's access is gone, the actor can mint a fresh login whenever they like.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Separation of duties: toxic combinations and two-person control
md: Separation of duties makes misuse require collusion. Write the conflicting pairs down, check requests against them (preventive), scan existing access (detective), and add a mitigating control wherever a split is impossible.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
md: A homography maps points only after dividing by the third coordinate. Code that multiplies by H and keeps the first two entries silently computes the wrong point everywhere except where W happens to be 1.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: The IR lifecycle: NIST 800-61r3, CSF 2.0 and SANS PICERL
md: Rev. 3's main shift is not new phases but a new framing: IR is part of everyday cybersecurity risk management, and improvement is continuous rather than a meeting at the end.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Memory forensics: processes, connections and injected code
md: Memory answers "what is running right now and talking to whom", which disk forensics cannot. That is why memory is captured first and why rebooting a suspect machine before capture is so costly.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: SQL injection step by step: watching the query change
md: Removing the word OR, or blocking the quote character, is not a fix. It breaks real users (O'Brien, a shop in Portland OR) and misses inputs that need neither, such as a numeric field (lesson 6). The fix is to stop building SQL text out of input.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: Completions can arrive in **any order**. The ring preserves the order in which requests are *attempted*, not the order in which they *finish*. Always identify a CQE by its `user_data` (often a pointer to your per-request state), never by its position.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Debug ports: UART, JTAG and SWD, and how makers lock them
md: Do not rely on hiding the pads (no labels, pins removed, epoxy). Those slow a curious owner and stop nobody determined. Treat physical obscurity as a delay, and make the chip itself refuse: burned debug fuses, disabled ROM download modes, no console login.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: One thread for every request: how Node.js runs JavaScript
md: Node.js runs all JavaScript for all users on one Event Loop in one process with the user's full privileges. That gives JavaScript servers two bug classes that matter more than elsewhere: input that blocks the loop (denial of service for everyone) and input that changes shared objects (a change that persists for every later request).

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: child_process: shells, arguments and Windows batch files
md: Prefer `execFile` or `spawn` with an argument array and no shell; put `--` before user-supplied values; validate values against an allowlist of expected forms; never combine an array with `shell: true`; and on Windows treat every batch file call as a shell call.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: mimalloc: three free lists per page
md: mimalloc replaces a per-thread cache with ownership: the thread that owns a page allocates and frees into it with plain loads and stores, and everyone else uses a per-page atomic list that the owner drains in batches.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
md: The search space is a product, so it grows exponentially in the number of knobs and linearly in the number of shapes you tune for. Any plan that says "just benchmark them all" has to survive that product.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
md: No IOMMU, no safety. `uio_pci_generic`, `igb_uio` and VFIO's `enable_unsafe_noiommu_mode` let the device DMA to any physical address. A bug in the application then corrupts the kernel or other processes: the ixy authors report losing a filesystem to rogue DMA writes on a misconfigured server. DPDK recommends vfio-pci with the IOMMU enabled.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
md: Epilogue fusion matters less than elementwise fusion for big GEMMs: the matmul is compute bound and dominates, so removing a 66 us kernel from a 947 us layer saves about 7 percent. It matters more for small or skinny matmuls, where the GEMM itself is short.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Matching what the teacher computes inside: hints, attention, states
md: Feature losses need alignment that output losses do not: a projection or regressor when widths differ (FitNets, TinyBERT's W_h), a layer mapping when depths differ, and the same spatial grid or the same token positions. Output distillation needs none of this, only the same set of classes or the same vocabulary.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Accumulated sums favor older tokens, which have had more steps to collect attention. In the toy, every later token entered with a tiny sum and was evicted within a few steps of leaving the recent slots.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: Offload tiers are a bigger prefix cache with the same keys. A hit is the longest contiguous prefix found across all tiers; everything after the first gap is prefill.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
md: HLC gives causality-respecting timestamps that look like wall time and fit in 64 bits. It does not make clocks agree: systems that need real-time guarantees still have to assume a skew bound and either wait it out (Spanner) or retry within it (CockroachDB).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
md: Misconception: Coconut does not shrink the model or skip layers. Each latent step is still a full forward pass through all layers. What it removes is the trip through the LM head, sampling and the embedding table between passes.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why superposition works: continuous thoughts and graph reachability
md: Read the theorem for what it is: a construction showing a 2-layer model with continuous thoughts *can* solve reachability in D steps, using embeddings as wide as the vocabulary. It does not show that a pretrained LLM learns this on GSM8k, and the matching experiments are small models trained from scratch on graph tasks.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: Do not read stage-0 output as a position. In the example it predicts 3.75 for key 1, which is at position 0. Stage 0 is graded only on whether it routes keys to leaves that can fit them, not on its own accuracy.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production
md: Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is not a cheap approximation of softmax attention that converges to it. The exponential kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (Katharopoulos et al.), so any finite state is a different, weaker model. That gap is what the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
md: A detail worth remembering for later: if a program's file is deleted while it is still running, `/proc/<pid>/exe` shows the original path with ` (deleted)` appended (`proc_pid_exe(5)`). Legitimate software rarely does this; a process running from a deleted file in `/tmp` is a classic sign of an intruder cleaning up after starting a tool.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Packages and updates, and the xz-utils backdoor
md: Patching closes most known holes, so do it promptly and automatically where you can, and reboot when the kernel or core libraries change. Package signatures protect the path from repository to you; they cannot vouch for the people upstream.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: One host is a checklist, a fleet is a control loop
md: A baseline you apply once decays. Write it down, apply it with an idempotent tool on a schedule, scan for drift, and stream telemetry off every host. The rest of this course fills in each box of that loop.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: The Linux audit system: how a system call becomes a record
md: Audit records come from the kernel, not the program, and one event is several records sharing TIME:SERIAL. auid (the login uid) is set once at login and survives su and sudo, which is what lets you attribute root actions to a person.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
md: Tetragon filters in the kernel and can act there. Hook LSM functions such as security_file_permission rather than raw system call arguments, start in observe mode, and pair Sigkill with Override when the operation itself must not happen.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair
md: Immutable does not mean uncompromisable. A remote bug still gives an attacker code execution in memory until the next reboot, and writable areas still persist. Keep runtime telemetry; immutability shrinks persistence, not intrusion.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Why open-ended output is hard to score
md: An evaluator is a measuring instrument. Before trusting any number it produces, check how often it agrees with careful human judgment on your task, at the level (single output or whole system) at which you will use it.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: policies, strengths and grounding
md: Read the coverage notes, not just the feature list. Per the AWS docs, sensitive information filters do not mask PII the model writes into tool call arguments, and grounding checks on a streamed response (one sent to the user piece by piece as it is generated) may mark it irrelevant only after it has been streamed. A guardrail protects only the channels it actually inspects.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Preemption is not free throughput. The optimistic policy's extra batch size is partly spent redoing prefills, and a preempted request's latency can jump by a full prefill plus queueing. Frequent preemption is a sign the pool is too small for the configured concurrency.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
md: Treat structured output as a contract with three checks: did it finish (stop reason), does it fit (schema, often enforced by the decoder), and is it right (your validators and evals, test sets of inputs with known good answers). Leave the model an honest way out, put reasoning before answers, and measure quality with and without the constraint.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
md: Misconception: "output is only 60 tokens, so it is negligible." For billing it is small. For latency it is not, because prefill reads thousands of tokens in parallel while decode produces tokens one step at a time.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Why use an LLM as the last-stage reranker
md: An LLM reranker is a prompt plus an aggregation rule. Pointwise, pairwise and listwise differ in what one call sees (1, 2 or a window of passages) and therefore in how many calls a ranking needs and how hard each call is.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris is invariant to rotation (eigenvalues do not change when the image rotates) but **not to scale**. Zoom in on a corner enough and, inside a fixed 3x3 window, it looks like an edge. Lesson 2 fixes this.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: Lock-free means a stalled thread can never stop the others: some operation always completes. It does not promise that any particular thread finishes, and it does not promise speed under contention.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
md: A common dodge: "I will write regexes only for the formats I care about and drop the rest." You cannot know in advance which format you will care about during the next incident, and the lines you dropped are exactly the rare error templates. Dropping them also silently biases every count you compute afterwards.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: What to log, source by source
md: Never write secrets into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet lists data to exclude or mask: passwords, access tokens, session identifiers (hash them if you need to follow a session), encryption keys, connection strings and sensitive personal data. Logs are copied widely, so anything in them leaks widely.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
md: Every allowlist entry is a promise that this pattern will never be malicious. Prefer fields the attacker cannot set (exact path in a protected folder, code-signing publisher, asset group from your inventory) over fields they can (process name, command-line text, user agent, file name).

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: YaRN = per-pair ramp on rotations $r = L/\lambda$ (keep fast pairs, fully interpolate slow ones, blend between) plus a logit temperature $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, all baked into the precomputed cos and sin tables.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
md: Dynamic halting is not free accuracy. It helped on bAbI and LAMBADA but slightly hurt translation, adds a ponder-cost hyperparameter, and makes different positions in a batch finish at different times.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
md: Looping buys **depth** (multi-step reasoning, using context), not **capacity** (memorized facts). Judge a looped model on reasoning tasks at matched FLOPs, not only on perplexity at matched parameters.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
md: Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: A model that passes forget-set benchmarks in full precision can fail them after an ordinary 4-bit conversion that a user applies for deployment. Any release that relies on unlearning should evaluate the quantized versions people will actually run.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Quarantine and Gatekeeper: the first-launch check
md: Gatekeeper is a first-launch, quarantine-triggered check. Removing the attribute (`xattr -d`), fetching with `curl`, or running a script through `bash` or `osascript` means it is never asked. Treat a process tree of browser or chat app, then Terminal, then curl, then shell or osascript as a detection signal, not as something Gatekeeper already covered.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: FileVault, secure boot and startup security
md: The SSV, SIP and FileVault protect each other. Apple notes the system will not let a user turn off the signed system volume while FileVault is on, because a tampered OS could capture the password at next boot. A baseline should require Full Security, SIP, SSV and FileVault together, and MDM should report any Mac that drops one.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Triage: hashes, magic bytes and strings
md: Strings lie by omission. Serious malware encrypts or encodes its strings and builds them at run time, so a short, clean strings list is not evidence of innocence. A file with almost no readable text at all is itself suspicious, as the packing lesson shows.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Packing, obfuscation and entropy
md: High entropy is a signal, not a verdict. Installers, compressed images in resources, and legitimately UPX-packed tools are high entropy too. Combine it with other signs: few imports, a writable and executable section, a raw size much smaller than the virtual size, or a section name that is not one of the usual ones.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number
md: Savings multiply, but so do quality losses. Each step (fewer dims, fewer bits) costs some recall, and the costs compound. Measure recall on your own queries at the exact size and precision you plan to serve, then use a rerank stage (next lesson) to win most of it back.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Context parallelism: balanced causal splits and the KV ring
md: CP splits every activation along the sequence. Megatron balances causal work by giving rank i chunks i and 2CP - 1 - i, and hides the KV ring when each GPU holds enough tokens: c at least 2(H_kv / H)(F / B).

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Virtual addresses, page tables and the DTB, walked by hand
md: If an entry's present bit is 0, the page is not in RAM: it may be in the page file, compressed, or never used. The data is then simply not in a raw image. Tools report such reads as invalid addresses or blank fields, and an absent value is not evidence that something did not exist.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Linux memory: banners, task lists, bash history and kernel checks
md: Linux images fail more often than Windows ones because of symbols. Before an incident, build or collect ISF files for the kernels you run (the volatility3-symbols project publishes some pre-generated ones), and record `uname -a` at collection so you know which banner to match. The `-u` (`--remote-isf-url`) option lets Volatility search an online ISF index; `--offline` stops all downloads.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: "Fragmentation is solved" is not the lesson. The study covers eight single-threaded C and C++ programs from the 1990s, and the authors call for more work on unusual program behaviour. Long-running servers with phase changes, many threads and per-thread caches are exactly that kind of workload, as the next lesson shows.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: `volatile` is not an ordering. In standard C++, volatile accesses are not atomic and do not order other memory, so they cannot be used for synchronization between threads. (MSVC, Microsoft's C++ compiler, gives volatile acquire/release semantics by default on x86 targets; that is a compiler extension, not the language.)

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Do not benchmark a reclamation scheme with one thread on an idle machine. The cost differences that matter, garbage growth under preemption and fence cost on long traversals, only appear with oversubscribed threads (more runnable threads than cores, so some are always preempted), update-heavy workloads and long data structures.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Integer overflow and signedness: when the size math lies
md: Every allocation size and every length passed to memcpy should come from a computation that cannot overflow and a value that cannot be negative. When a size comes from a file or a packet, validate it against the real data first.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Batch hard needs K of at least 2, or there is no positive to take a max over. And because it always picks the extreme pair, label noise and outlier crops dominate the loss: Hermans and colleagues show such outliers in Market-1501 and MARS (a video-based re-ID dataset) in their supplementary material.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Repeat, interleave, and report the mean with a confidence interval (or a median with its spread). Never decide from one run or from the best of N.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
md: TITO fixes which tokens are trained on, R3 fixes which experts process them, and the precision contract fixes how each matmul is quantized. Each removes one cause of the importance ratio drifting away from 1.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
md: Misconception: "we never exported that activity, so it is not exported." Libraries add components to the merged manifest at build time. Review the manifest of the APK you ship (lesson 3), not the one in your repository.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
